Observer lets one object announce that something happened to any number of others without knowing what they do about it. The object making the announcement is the
; each one registers itself with the subject through
, and the subject calls every registered listener when its event occurs, through

The problem is code that would otherwise call each interested party by name: a battery monitor that has to know about the logger, the low-voltage alarm and the dashboard individually, and gains a new parameter every time a fourth thing needs to react. Observer inverts that: the subject knows only that some list of listeners exists, and a new listener is one more subscription, not one more parameter anywhere.
The mechanism is a list the subject holds and walks on every event, calling each listener in turn. Two shapes for the call exist.
hands the listener the data itself, simple to call but tying every listener to the exact shape the subject sends.
only says something changed, and the listener reads what it needs by calling back into the subject, which frees the payload from the subject's own type at the cost of an extra call per listener.

What it costs is not the call, it is lifetime. A listener destroyed without unsubscribing leaves the subject holding a pointer to nothing, and a listener that unsubscribes itself from inside its own callback can corrupt the list the subject is in the middle of walking. Both are solved by never handing the subject something it can dereference after it stops being valid: a
locked before every call, or a removal deferred until the walk is over.

You meet this in a ROS 2 subscription, where a callback fires for every message a publisher sends, and the interview question is exactly the lifetime half of it: sketch subscribe and unsubscribe, and say what happens when a listener goes first.

c.v: The erase after the loop is safe because nothing is reading
at that point: every callback that was going to run this round has already returned, so

shifts and destroys entries in a container no call frame still has a reference into. Erasing during the loop is dangerous specifically because the entry being removed can be the one whose code is still executing; erasing after the loop removes only entries that have already finished being used, which is a fact about time, not about which container operation is doing the erasing.
